rv.q: The switch from romp-com to dramedy is slightly jarring, as slapstick farce – including a slow-motion fight – prevails throughout.
Ajay Chowdhury's direction struggles to find the balance between serious and childish, with some scenes being too immature and others not having the weight they should.
This odd little show has charm aplenty, though for some it may also prove something of a well-intentioned dog’s dinner.
Giving human voices to pets was something of a double-edged sword in this case.
This is bold comedy-drama, centering middle-aged females (and their dogs).
Every dog has its day and, if the audience’s warm, laughter-filled reaction is anything to go by, this play will certainly have many more bright days in its future.
It's a charming, funny, surprising and heartfelt production that leaves the audience with plenty of emotional jolts, both happy and sad.
Dog Mom , is an offbeat and heartfelt comedy about starting over, finding your people, and learning that love occasionally arrives covered in mud and playful chaos.
Dog Mom is a charming, if somewhat uneven, production... the production never quite turns its charming premise into something theatrically distinctive.
Dog Mom has bags of heart, but it could dig deeper.
A funny, occasionally touching comedy that runs out of steam before the finish.
But she is not enough to save the show.
By taking itself a touch too seriously, “Dog Mom” weakens the messages that are better served with humour.
Its shallowness is what ultimately seals the play's fate.
Ultimately, DOG MOM has an enormous amount of heart and a fiercely talented physical cast who are working their absolute tails off.
The story beats are telegraphed early, and the play's sad conclusion is far too bloated for the story it is trying to tell.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this whimsical comedy about a divorced woman and talking dogs, with some charmed by the heartfelt performances and canine antics, while others find the concept gimmicky and the pacing uneven.
